1317.title: Predicting the end
1317.hook: people have set dates, like the Millerites; Jesus said no one knows the hour
1317.howItsDone: Churches that say the Nicene Creed confess that Christ will come again, and some Christians read Matthew 24 in Advent as a call to watchfulness rather than a timetable.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul's letter to grieving friends. Your line was ever with the Lord.

A preacher named William Miller sat down with the book of Daniel and a lot of arithmetic, and worked out when Christ would return. People believed him, and among his followers a day was fixed. They told their neighbors and waited. The day came, and the sun went down on it like any other. His followers gave what came next a name: the Great Disappointment. Others have set dates too, and each one has come and gone. Yet the Gospels record Jesus saying something very plain about that day, plain enough for a sticky note.

First, the plain words. In Matthew, on the Mount of Olives, Jesus says: "But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only." In Mark, the King James text adds, "neither the Son." Christians explain that line in different ways, but the sentence is hard to miss: not you, not the angels. Second, the thief. Paul tells the Thessalonians "the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night." A thief doesn't send a schedule. In Acts, when the disciples ask the risen Jesus whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel, he answers: "It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power." Then he's taken up, and two men in white ask, "why stand ye gazing up into heaven?" Third, what to do instead: "Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come." Right after, Jesus tells of a servant left in charge of a household: "Blessed is that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing." Doing what? His job, feeding the household on time. Watching here isn't staring at the sky with a calculator. It's being found at your work, faithful, whenever the knock comes. Fourth, fear. Date-setting can run on dread and on excitement, and both can pull people out of their ordinary lives. Not knowing the hour sends attention back to this one: the people in the house, the work in front of you.
screen: `NOT THE ANGELS, BUT THE FATHER ONLY.`

segments.voice: Name one fear about the end, once and quietly, about the world or your own life: a diagnosis, a deadline, a headline. Picture setting it down on a table beside you like a bag carried too long, and without arguing with it, bring your attention to this hour: the room, the sounds, the next ordinary thing you'll do. If you pray, hand the fear over to God; if not, just leave it on the table.
Predicting the end. People have set dates, and the dates have passed. In the Gospels Jesus says of that day and hour, no one knows.
Your line: no one knows the hour. Not the angels, and not the date-setters. Same time tomorrow.

1318.title: The apocalypse in art
1318.hook: the Angers tapestry, Dürer's woodcuts: artists pictured Revelation vividly
1318.tomorrow: When the saints go marching in
1318.howItsDone: Christians have pictured Revelation in tapestries, illuminated manuscripts, woodcuts, paintings and stained glass, and some churches and museums display these works for people to look at and pray with.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dates people set for the end, and Jesus's plain words about that day. Your line was no one knows the hour.

In a castle in the French city of Angers hangs a tapestry of the book of Revelation, woven in wool, so long you see it by walking beside it, scene after scene: angels with trumpets, the dragon, the beast, the holy city coming down. In Germany, the artist Albrecht Dürer made Revelation into woodcuts and printed it, and his four horsemen gallop off the page together. Painters, weavers, glassmakers and printers have kept turning this book into pictures. Why does it lend itself to the eye, and what do the pictures uncover?

First, the name. The book opens, in the King James, "The Revelation of Jesus Christ." The Greek word there is apokalypsis: an uncovering, an unveiling. In the text, apocalypse doesn't mean disaster. It means a curtain pulled back. Second, the book is already a picture book. Again and again John says I saw, I beheld, I looked. In chapter six, as the seals open, the horses come one by one: white, red, black, and then: "And I looked, and behold a pale horse: and his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him." Colors, riders, crowns, scales. An artist barely has to invent anything. Third, every picture is a reading. Which scene? How frightening? Do the horsemen come one by one, as the text has them, or charge together, as Dürer drew them, one wave thundering over the people below? The dragon, or the woman it can't destroy? Some artists dwelt on the terror; some gave as much room to the river, the tree and the open city. A tapestry or a woodcut shows what its maker heard in the book, and often what the maker's own time feared and hoped. Fourth, why it matters. A picture can do what the book does: hold back the ordinary for a moment and uncover something. Some people meet Revelation first through an image, and a pale horse on a print can send a reader to look up chapter six.
screen: `AN IMAGE SENDS YOU TO THE TEXT.`

segments.voice: Find one image from Revelation, Dürer's Four Horsemen, a panel of the Angers tapestry, a picture in a Bible, or simply picture this week's city with open gates. Look, without reading about it, until you find one detail you missed at first glance. Then ask what the artist was afraid of, and what the artist hoped for; if you pray, let the image become a prayer without words.
The apocalypse in art. Tapestry, woodcut, paint and glass: artists turning John's I saw into pictures, each one a reading of the book.
Your line: art unveils. Every picture of the book is someone's reading of it. Until tomorrow.

1319.title: When the saints go marching in
1319.word: When the saints go marching in
1319.hook: spirituals turned Revelation into hope: wanting to be in that number
1319.howItsDone: When the Saints Go Marching In is sung in some churches and played by brass bands, including at funerals in New Orleans, and some churches read Revelation 7:9–17 on All Saints' Day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Revelation in wool and woodcut, every picture a reading. Your line was art unveils.

A brass band starts up on a street. A trombone slides, a drum kicks in, and people who were only watching fall in behind. The tune is When the Saints Go Marching In, sung slow in churches and played fast by bands, and nobody can say for certain who first sang it. Under the bounce there's one plain wish: when the saints go marching in on the last day, the singer wants to be in that number. Counted. Not watching from the curb. Some listeners hear that number in the seventh chapter of Revelation.

First, the number John hears: "And I heard the number of them which were sealed: and there were sealed an hundred and forty and four thousand of all the tribes of the children of Israel." A precise count, tribe by tribe. Second, what John sees when he looks up: "After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands." He hears a number, then sees a crowd nobody can count. Christians explain the two as two groups, or as one people seen two ways. Third, who they are. An elder tells John: "These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb." People who came through hard things. And the chapter ends with a line this block has met before: "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes." Fourth, who counts as a saint. In Paul's letters the word means a church's members: "to all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi." Catholic and Orthodox Christians, and some Protestants, also honor particular saints by name, with feast days; other Protestants keep the word mostly for the whole church. Either way, the song isn't about a few famous names. Other spirituals sing Bible pictures as present hope too: a chariot swinging low, a balm in Gilead. This one puts the singer in the crowd before the throne.

Sing or hum the song softly and slowly, more hymn than parade, or hum any tune you love if you don't know it. Between the lines, bring to mind the people you'd want in that number with you, someone who taught you, someone who came through something hard, someone you've lost, and let the crowd grow past what you can count. If you pray, hold them before God; if not, just sing them in.
When the saints go marching in. A song with one wish, to be counted among the saints, and, some hear, Revelation's multitude which no man could number.

1320.title: Hope, not fear
1320.hook: Christian hope is trust that God finishes what he begins (Philippians 1:6)
1320.howItsDone: Christians name hope among faith, hope and love (1 Corinthians 13:13), and some memorize Philippians 1:6 or pray it for people going through a long, unfinished season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a brass-band song and a multitude no one could number. Your line was in that number.

The letter was written in chains. Paul tells the church at Philippi that his "bonds in Christ are manifest in all the palace." He writes as a man who might live or die; a few lines later he weighs both, and says he's torn. You'd expect a letter like that to open with worry, or a request for help. Instead, almost the first thing he writes is a sentence with no doubt in it at all, about somebody else's unfinished life. Today's word is what some Christians say all of Revelation is meant to give.
screen: `A SENTENCE WITH NO DOUBT IN IT.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence: "Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ." Perform, in the old English, means carry it through to the end. The confidence isn't in the Philippians, still a work in progress, or in Paul, in prison. It rests on the one who began. Second, hope isn't the same as optimism. Paul in bonds isn't forecasting good news; he says plainly, "to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain." Hebrews puts it this way: "Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." And Paul tells the Romans, "hope that is seen is not hope." Hope looks past what can be seen yet, to who holds the ending. Third, hope and fear. Revelation can be read as a book of threats, and some people have met it that way. But this block kept arriving at the same places: all things new, open gates, healing leaves, come, Lord Jesus. The first letter of John says, "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear." Fear asks what will go wrong. Hope asks who is finishing the story. Fourth, unfinished people. Paul isn't embarrassed that the Philippians are half-built. He expects it. Some Christians bring this verse to people in the middle of things: a recovery, a grief, a slow change that hasn't arrived. The work isn't done. On Paul's account, it will be.
screen: `HE WHICH HATH BEGUN WILL PERFORM IT.`
`HOPE THAT IS SEEN IS NOT HOPE.`

segments.voice: Let one worry about something unfinished come up, your health, a child, your work, yourself, without rehearsing it. Then look in that same place for something already begun, a first step, a small mercy, someone who showed up, and hold it beside the fear without needing the fear to disappear. If you pray, rest on Paul's words, he which hath begun a good work; if not, keep both in view and breathe.
Hope. Not a guess that things will turn out fine, but trust, written from chains, that the one who began a good work will carry it through.
Your line: he will finish it. Hope rests on the one who began. See you tomorrow.

1321.title: Remember you will die
1321.hook: tradition says monks kept skulls on their desks to value each day
1321.howItsDone: On Ash Wednesday, Catholic and some Protestant churches mark ashes on the forehead, sometimes with the words 'remember that thou art dust'; some Christians also pray Psalm 90 at funerals or at the turn of the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hope written from chains. Your line was he will finish it.

A skull on a writing desk, beside the candle and the open book. Tradition says some monks kept one there, not to be gloomy, but to be reminded. In old paintings a skull sometimes sits beside a saint at prayer, as calm as an inkwell. But the Bible has a prayer that asks for the same reminder, without bones on the desk. Its heading calls it "A Prayer of Moses the man of God." Today's word is a Latin phrase for what the skull was saying.

First, the request. Psalm ninety, which day one thousand read for its thousand years, asks: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." Not count your years. Number your days. And it's asked as a lesson, teach us, not handed down as a threat. The point of the counting is a wiser heart. Second, how short. The same psalm says people are like grass: "In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth." And: "we spend our years as a tale that is told." James asks outright: "For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away." Third, the Latin. Memento mori: remember that you will die. Not a Bible verse, but a saying Christians kept close to the Bible's words. Some churches put it in the body. On Ash Wednesday, in Catholic and some Protestant churches, a minister marks ashes on the forehead, sometimes with words from Genesis: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." Other churches don't keep the day. Fourth, why want this? Ecclesiastes says it's better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting, because the living will lay it to heart. Remembering the end sorts what matters from what doesn't. In this block it sits beside everything else: dust, and all things new. On the desk, the skull sat beside an open book.

Think of your own death gently for about a minute, your life as a tale that is told; if today is hard for that, or you're grieving, number just this one day. Then ask what would make today count: a call, an apology, an hour given to someone. If you pray, say teach us to number our days; if not, hold the day in your hands. If thoughts of death feel heavy or dark, you don't have to carry them alone: call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Memento mori. Latin: remember that you will die. Kept close to Psalm ninety's prayer, teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
Your line: number your days. Not as a threat, but as a lesson. I'll be here tomorrow.

1322.title: The art of dying
1322.hook: medieval handbooks taught how to die well: with faith, forgiveness and company
1322.howItsDone: In Catholic and Orthodox churches a priest may be called to anoint and pray with the dying; in Protestant churches a pastor and family may gather at the bedside to read scripture, pray and say goodbye.

segments.voice: Yesterday, memento mori: remember that you will die, kept beside Psalm ninety's prayer. Your line was number your days.

A man lies in bed, and the room is crowded. In the old woodcuts, small demons crouch on the blanket, holding up scrolls of temptation: you've done too much wrong, it's too late, hold on to your money. On the other side, angels lean in, and saints stand at the bedside. The man barely moves; everything happens around him, and all of it is about him. The pictures come from little handbooks made in medieval Europe and passed from hand to hand, so ordinary people, not only priests, would know what to do when someone was dying.
screen: `DEMONS ON ONE SIDE, ANGELS ON THE OTHER.`

segments.voice: Ars moriendi means the art of dying. It sounds grim, but the handbooks were trying to be kind. First, it was practical. A priest might not arrive in time, so the books told friends and family what to say and do. Nobody was supposed to die alone; company was part of the art. Second, the temptations. The books named the fears that come at the end, among them despair: the thought that it's too late for mercy. Their answer came from the Gospels. One of the men crucified beside Jesus, with nothing left to offer, says, "Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." Jesus answers, "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." If it wasn't too late for him, the books said, it isn't too late for you. Third, forgiveness: settle what you can, ask pardon and give it. The model again was the cross, where Jesus prays, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." Fourth, the turn: you can't learn an art on the last day. The handbooks were read by the healthy too. To forgive at the end, practice forgiving now; to trust at the end, practice trusting on a Tuesday. Dying well, they thought, is mostly the shape of how you lived. Christians still keep pieces of this. Catholic and Orthodox families may call a priest for anointing and last prayers; Protestant families may gather to read scripture and pray at the bedside. The tools differ. The idea is the same: nobody should face it unready, or alone.

Let one grudge come up, not the biggest in your life, a medium one you've carried longer than it deserves, and for this minute try loosening your hold on it. If you pray, you can use the words from the cross, Father, forgive them; if not, simply let your grip loosen a little. If despair ever feels close, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Ars moriendi. Latin for the art of dying: old handbooks teaching faith, forgiveness and company at the end of a life.
Your line: die well, live well. The art is learned on ordinary days. Go gently.

1323.title: Funerals
1323.hook: from Orthodox memory eternal to Protestant celebrations of life
1323.howItsDone: Orthodox funerals and memorial services end with the hymn Memory Eternal; Catholics celebrate a funeral Mass; Protestant churches hold a service of worship with hymns, scripture and remembrance, sometimes called a celebration of life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ars moriendi, the art of dying: faith against despair, forgiveness, and company. Your line was die well, live well.

Two funerals on the same Saturday. In an Orthodox church, the coffin is open, candles are lit in every hand, and the air is thick with incense. At the end the choir sings one short line, slow and low, again and again, and the whole room joins in. Across town, in a Protestant church, there's a slideshow: a man at a barbecue, a man holding a grandchild, a man in a terrible sweater. People laugh. Someone reads a poem. A friend tells a story about a fishing trip that went wrong. Two rooms, two moods, the same faith underneath.

A Christian funeral does two jobs at once: it grieves a person, and it says out loud what the church hopes. Churches balance those jobs differently. First, the Orthodox. Their funeral and memorial services end with a short hymn, memory eternal. It sounds like a wish that people won't forget, but it asks God to remember the one who has died. In Genesis, "God remembered Noah," and the next thing God does is make a wind pass over the earth, and the waters go down. Second, the Catholic funeral Mass. The body is brought into church, often sprinkled with holy water and covered with a white cloth that recalls baptism, and the Mass is offered for the person who has died. Third, Protestant churches: a service of witness to the resurrection, or what some families call a celebration of life, with hymns, scripture, and stories that bring the person back into the room for an hour. Fourth, what they share. At the graveside, an old English prayer book has the minister commit the body "earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust; in sure and certain hope of the Resurrection to eternal life." The same book opens its burial service with words Jesus spoke to Martha, on his way to her brother Lazarus's grave: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live." Candles or slideshows, tears or laughter, usually both. Underneath, the same claim: this person is not lost to God.
screen: `EARTH TO EARTH, IN SURE AND CERTAIN HOPE.`

segments.voice: Bring back one funeral you went to, and then the person, in one clear detail: a laugh, a habit, a phrase they used. If you pray, say their name to God and ask God to remember them; if not, simply keep their memory company for a minute. If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Funerals. The church grieving a person and naming its hope in the same hour.
Your line: memory eternal. Not only that we remember, but that God does. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: My friend's family is holding a celebration of life. Is that a real Christian funeral?
options: Yes. Churches balance grief and hope differently, but all say the person isn't lost to God.
No. Only a service with incense and an open coffin counts as a Christian funeral.
Not really. A Christian funeral is for grief alone, never for laughter or stories.
chat.meaning: Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant funerals look different, but each grieves a person and says the same hope: this person is not lost to God.
